I wasn't going to step back into that house, and it took me this long to get my family out. Our vacation had morphed into a slow-motion nightmare, and now it was time to cut our losses. I could still feel cold fingers on the back of my neck, and it took every ounce of my sanity to rationalize that away.

I saw my most stubborn niece out of the corner of my eye, dart back inside. Shit. My brother, the attentive father he was, immediately jumped into action, and vanished behind the doorway. I reasoned with the rest of my large clan that we had to go, that we could meet up with him later. I left unsaid the feeling that we were lucky to have made it out the door in one unit. In one piece.

My father, just as attentive, said he'd poke his head in to examine the situation. Me, being the horror fanatic, knew this is how we split off, one by one, to be consumed by some nebulous evil. I told him I wasn't letting him near that doorway without locking arms, and letting me brace myself on the outer frame. He looked at me like I was mad, but I didn't care. I know what I felt.

Arm in arm, he leaned in the doorway and peered for an uncomfortable minute, and at one point I pulled him out solely by fear reflex, and asked what he saw. He leaned back in the frame, and then his head swiveled toward me in the most unnatural-looking angle, and said in a calm, unnerving voice, that everything was fine, my brother was merely crawling across the ceiling.

With that I yanked him out of the doorway just as the heavy door rapped closed, hard enough to have separated us at the shoulders had I not acted. Whatever that was, snapped him out of his daze, and we tripped over each other retreating off the porch.

I ushered them into the van they rented to transport the majority of us, and they demanded I travel with them, which I didn't argue. I don't think there is anything wrong with finding pleasure in getting new things, it is exciting and rewarding. I think what you may be wanting is an appreciation for the things you already have. Look around you, find things that you truly cherish or use frequently. If you don't use/need it, or it's not sentimental go ahead and put it in a garbage bag or something (start with a few, small/insignificant items). If you dont use it or miss it in a month donate it to charity without looking into the bag. Chances are you will forget what it is by the time a month is up and if you look at it then you may convince yourself that you still need it (I've done that myself). You will feel a good knowing that your items are going to be useful to someone else and you slowly free yourself from the burden your stuff has on you.

Another thing you can try is getting rid of as many items as you purchase. So if you purchase new clothes (for example), donate the same number of clothing that you don't wear much, or like anymore. This way there is a kind of weight, to each purchase. To gain something, you must also lose something

Just to clarify, I'm not suggesting you get of all your stuff. I dont think its wrong to get new things, or to have luxury items. But I have found that the more I have, the less satisfied I become with each individual item. It also makes it so that when I purchase a new item it is really meaningful and I can have peace of mind that I'm not wasting my money on things I dont need. (also sorry for the wall of text)
Before you buy something, imagine the product in one hand and the cash amount the product costs in the other hand. Which hand would you grab? The cash amount or the product?

Every item you buy, it's an item you will have to maintain, clean and store somewhere. When you move, you will have to sell it or find a way to haul it with you.

If you are the type to get attached to inanimate items, you will feel a bit of emotional pain at the idea of letting that item go if and when you have to part with it.

When you are in stores, hold on to thoughts of that hassle, clutter and pain. By the active choice not to buy, you escape all of those things.

The less I have, the more I gain.

I try to tackle this hurdle by visualizing and planning the activities I'll use the product for, once I've got it.

It provides me with a perspective and an incentive. With a bit of training it keeps me on my toes, knowing what I really want to buy and that I want to maintain the product well. Also, because I like the things I'm going to use it for, I'm more motivated to research the best stuff, so I don't waste my money on junk. If that means to spend twice as much to get a product that lasts 5 times as long, I find the funds to bite the bullet.

Right now I'm contemplating dropping 140 euros for a pair of Fjallraven pants, which will last me about 5 years. I'll use them extensively, while camping and hiking, and with that perspective in mind the price drops steeply, compared to 90 euros for a pair of jeans that last me about a year.

Rethink retailers as a honey-trap, which they are. But that doesn't mean you don't need stuff or take pleasure in the hunt for things. It's primal, just don't go broke doing it.
